newsitem.title: UK: Smart cards to revolutionise health care - journal.
newsitem.headline: Smart cards to revolutionise health care - journal.

text.p: Smart cards that carry patient data and ensure only legitimate doctors access medical records will soon revolutionise health care, a British expert predicted on Friday.

The cards containing a tiny computer chip would allow patients to see their own records and let doctors easily exchange information about a patient, Roderick Neame, who manages Health Information Consulting, argued in the British Medical Journal.
"Smart cards are set to play a pivotal role in the future development of computing in general, and particularly in health care," Neame wrote.

Smart cards are used in digital mobile telephones, satellite broadcast receivers, on supermarket "loyalty" cards that keep track of purchases and in systems where cards act as cash, such as Britain's Mondex system.
Neame said about 90 million health smart cards were in use in France, Canada, Germany and Britain.
The cards allow patient information to be accessed via computer only when the card and the right Personal Identification Number (PIN) were used.
"A patient's smart card would point' to the records belonging to the patient, enabling a doctor to retrieve them as required," Neame wrote.

Because of the security of the system, Neame said, patient records could be available via the Internet. "This means they could be accessed readily with cheap browser software using cheap communications networks," he wrote.
"The potential to exchange medical records within and between service providers...would be achievable at low cost."
Patients could control who saw their records, Neame said.

"What is more, this could enable the goal of patient empowerment' to be achieved at the same time; patients could control access to their own personalised records, as well as reading them when they chose to do so or when they wished to seek an independent audit or review of their care."
